name: Kurtöp
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_citation: Hyslop, Gwendolyn. 2011. A Grammar of Kurtöp. PhD dissertation, University of Oregon, Eugene. xxxix+729 pp. (open access, UO Scholars' Bank). Corroborated by Hyslop, Gwendolyn. 2021. Between Stress and Tone: Acoustic Evidence of Word Prominence in Kurtöp. Language Documentation & Conservation 15: 551-575 (open access, ScholarSpace, hdl 10125/74668).
catalog_quote: Kurtöp is another example of a tonal language that also has word-level stress and I argue that stressed syllables in Kurtöp can be identified by the following properties: 1) the obligatory presence of high or low tone; 2) the possibility of a complex onset or long vowel; and 3) the acoustic correlate of duration. ... In summary, the first syllable of words must bear a tone (either high or low). This obligatory presence of tone is a feature of Kurtöp stress. In addition to the obligatory presence of tone, stressed syllables are slightly longer. ... External evidence for first-syllable stress in Kurtöp comes from several sources. First is the intution I share with native speakers that first sysllables are somehow more prominent than other syllables. Second is the movement of tone to the leftmost edge of the word (i.e. the first syllable) when prefixed. ... [p. 204] The primary acoustic correlates of Kurtöp stress are duration and tone. ... [p. 226] In Kurtöp, phonological words can be identified by first syllable stress and the obligatory presence of tone. ... [Hyslop 2021: 557] Without exception, the initial syllable of the root is stressed. This will be the first syllable of the word, except in negated verbs, in which case stress is found on the second syllable. Negation is done by way of a prefix (the only prefix in the language; all other affixes are suffixes), but stress remains on the initial syllable of the verb stem.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kurtöp has lexical tone (H vs L, contrastive only after sonorant onsets, realized on the first syllable) plus word-level stress fixed on the first syllable of the phonological word; the stressed initial syllable obligatorily bears the H/L tone, alone licenses complex onsets and long vowels, and is longer (~10 ms) than the second syllable; intensity and vowel quality are not correlates.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described. Synchronically transparent noun compounds (e.g. phokhwi 'male dog') are said to have 'compound stress' as opposed to 'normal stress' (§11.3.2, p. 294), without further detail.
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote 79 (p. 247), added after the defense: in verbal negation stress appears to stay stem-initial and does not shift to the negative prefix má-, whereas tone does shift to the prefix — i.e. stress is stem-initial rather than strictly word-initial when a prefix is present (prefixes are otherwise rare). Bound suffixes/enclitics (e.g. -the) do not receive their own stress but are incorporated into the host word's stress pattern (p. ~310).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (grammatical word plus optional particle/enclitics), §7.4 p. 226; evidence includes a production study of disyllabic words in a carrier frame (§7.2.1). Language is analysed as tonal-with-stress in Hyman's (2006) typology.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Kurtöp (ISO xkz, Glottolog kurt1248 'Kurtokha') as spoken in Dungkar geok, Lhuentse district, Bhutan; same languoid as the target. No dialect restriction relevant to the stress statement.
